title: Flags, Lazy Quantifiers & Complex Pattern Matching
description: Master execution flags, lazy quantifiers (`*?`, `+?`, `??`), and complex real-world string parsing while avoiding catastrophic backtracking.

primer.definition: Lazy quantifiers (*?, +?, ??) match the shortest possible substring required to satisfy the expression instead of greedily expanding. Flags modify engine execution behavior globally across the whole pattern: /i ignores letter case, /m changes where ^ and $ anchor, /s lets . match newlines, and /u switches the engine to full Unicode mode.
primer.goldenRule: Use lazy quantifiers when capturing content bounded by explicit delimiters (like quotes, backticks, or HTML tags) to prevent over-matching across multiple adjacent occurrences.
primer.mentalModel: Picture two independent dials on the regex engine. One dial controls each quantifier's appetite -- greedy quantifiers grab as much as possible then backtrack down, lazy quantifiers (`*?`, `+?`, `??`) grab as little as possible then expand only if forced. The other dial is a bank of switches you flip once per pattern -- flags like /i, /m, /s, /u -- that change how `.`, `^`, `$`, and character classes behave for the entire match, completely independent of which quantifiers you chose.
points: Lazy quantifiers (*?, +?, ??) still backtrack like their greedy counterparts -- they just start from the minimum count and expand outward instead of starting from the maximum and shrinking inward.

Flags are set once per pattern (e.g. the second argument to `new RegExp(pattern, flags)`, or the letters after the closing slash in a /pattern/flags literal) and apply to the whole match, not to an individual token.

The i flag makes letter comparisons case-insensitive; the m flag makes ^ and $ match at every line boundary instead of only the start/end of the whole string; the s flag (dotAll) makes . match newline characters, which it otherwise never does; the u flag switches the engine to full Unicode mode, enabling \p{...} property escapes and correct handling of astral characters.
Flags can be combined in any order in the same flags string, e.g. "gim" or "su".
pitfalls: Forgetting the m flag is the most common cause of a ^ or $ anchor silently failing on multi-line input -- without it, ^ and $ only match the very start and end of the entire string, not each line.

The s (dotAll) flag is easy to confuse with the m (multiline) flag -- s changes what `.` matches, m changes what `^`/`$` match; they solve different problems and are often needed together for multi-line block content.

Lazy quantifiers do not guarantee correctness by themselves -- `.*?` next to the wrong delimiter can still under-match or over-match; laziness only changes which match is returned when multiple are possible, not whether the pattern is otherwise correct.
Using \p{...} unicode property escapes without the u flag is either a syntax error or silently treated as literal characters depending on the engine -- always pair \p{...} with u.

examples.note: Lazy + stops at the first '>' instead of consuming through the last '>' in a string with multiple tags.
The i flag makes the literal match case-insensitively.
The m flag lets ^ and $ anchor to each line inside a multi-line string, instead of only the whole string's start and end.
The s flag makes '.' match the newline between 'a' and 'b', which it would otherwise skip.

cards.prompt: Match 'a' followed by as few characters as possible until 'b' using lazy quantifier `.*?`.

testCases.description: Empty string cannot satisfy the literal 'a' and 'b' boundaries.

cards.prompt: Match the start of any line beginning with 'ERROR:' inside a multi-line log using ^ anchored per-line via the /m flag.

testCases.description: ^ matches right after each newline only because the m flag is set; without it, ^ only anchors to the very start of the whole string.

cards.prompt: Match content wrapped in '<<<' and '>>>' delimiters that may span multiple lines, using a lazy dot that matches newlines via the /s flag.

testCases.description: . matches the embedded newline only because the s (dotAll) flag is set; without it, . never matches \n.

testCases.description: \p{L} matches these unicode letters only because the u flag enables unicode property escapes.
